hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up on $[(4 + 2) \div 3] \times [10 - (2 \times 3)]$. Left bracket: $6 \div 3 = 2$. Right bracket: $10 - 6 = 4$. Then $2 \times 4 = 8$. Same two-bracket plan below.
There are two brackets multiplied together. Treat each bracket as its own small problem before multiplying.
Left bracket: $18 + 6 = 24$, then $24 \div 3$. Right bracket: $2 \times 4 = 8$, then $15 - 8$. Multiply your two results.
The left bracket is $8$ and the right bracket is $7$, and $8 \times 7 = 56$, so the expression equals $56$.

explanation: In the left bracket, the parentheses go first: $18 + 6 = 24$, and then $24 \div 3 = 8$.
In the right bracket, the parentheses go first: $2 \times 4 = 8$, and then $15 - 8 = 7$.
Now multiply the two finished brackets: $8 \times 7 = 56$.
The whole expression has a value of $56$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Write it as a shrinking line
⚠️ The trap here
steps: A very common wrong answer is $140$: that comes from reading the left bracket as $18 + 6 \div 3 = 18 + 2 = 20$, then $20 \times 7$.
The inner parentheses around $18 + 6$ are exactly what stops that — they say add first, divide second.
Escape it by copying the expression and physically crossing out each pair of parentheses as you finish it, so you never skip one.
